title: Anthropic and Theorem Labs use Claude to formally verify 123 open-source libraries
subtitle: Claude produced ~180 million lines of mechanically-checked Rocq proofs covering 239 entry points across 123 libraries — and surfaced bugs that trillions of fuzzing runs had missed.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team and Theorem Labs published results on October 22 from a large-scale experiment in using Claude for formal software verification. The team wrote proofs for 239 entry points across 123 open-source libraries — roughly 180 million lines of proof code — using Claude to generate proofs in the Rocq proof assistant, which then mechanically verified each one. The pipeline reused existing OSS-Fuzz fuzz tests as the source of formal specifications.

The headline result is that the proofs uncovered hundreds of bugs that fuzzing — with trillions of runs behind it — had never surfaced. Formal verification proves the absence of a class of bugs under the specification, where fuzzing can only sample inputs; so when the two disagree, formal verification is in principle more informative. What has historically limited it is cost: writing proofs is slow, expensive expert work. Automating the proof-writing step with a frontier model is what makes a 180M-line effort tractable at all.

Anthropic is explicit about the limits. 'Formally verified' here means the single-threaded, static RISC-V binary meets a specification derived from an existing fuzz harness; it does not mean the x86 or ARM target most code actually ships on is bug-free, and it does not address concurrency, memory models beyond the proof's assumptions, or specification bugs themselves. Still, the shape of the result matters: AI-assisted formal methods are moving from research demos onto the open-source supply chain.

A note for learners: this is the kind of result that quietly reshapes an entire discipline. If you have been told formal verification is academic and impractical, update that prior. The useful skills over the next few years are reading specifications, understanding what a proof actually guarantees, and knowing where the gap between the proof and the shipped binary lives. Those are not model-training skills — they are software engineering, and they transfer.
